## Abstract
Increasing concern about the cost and value of higher education has increased interest in understanding how institutional characteristics, and cost relate to student outcomes, particularly earning after graduation. This project uses institution-level data from the U.S. Department of Education’s College Scorecard to investigate how tuition, institutional features, and student enrollment are associated with median earnings 10 years after enrollment. Additionally, it aims to assess the extent to which these variables can predict higher-earning graduates. 

The dataset is restricted to institutions that primarily award bachelor’s degrees, and report complete information on 10-year earnings and core cost and outcome variables. After filtering and cleaning, the resulting sample retains a diverse set of institutions across regions, control types, and locale categories. To model earnings as a continuous outcome, the project applies both ordinary least squares (OLS) and Ridge regression. The OLS model explains a substantial portion of the variation in 10-year earnings, with retention, completion, and in-state tuition emerging as strong positive predictors, and median debt and Pell share showing negative associations. Ridge regression provides comparable predictive accuracy while better handling multicollinearity among financial variables.

A classification task reframes the problem by labeling institutions as high-earning or low-earning relative to the sample median. Feature selection using statistical tests, random forest importance, and permutation importance identifies a consistent set of influential predictors, including enrollment size, retention, completion, tuition, and Pell share. Logistic regression and random forest models are then trained on the selected feature set. Both models achieve strong performance, with F1 scores around 0.77–0.82. Calibration curves show that each model produces reasonably reliable probability estimates, with logistic regression slightly smoother and more aligned with observed frequencies.

Overall, the results suggest that while tuition contributes to differences in earnings, institutional performance indicators and student composition play a larger role. Earnings outcomes reflect a combination of institutional characteristics and the demographic and academic profile of the students they serve, highlighting the complexity of evaluating value in higher education.

***
## Introduction
The rising cost of higher education in the United States has intensified concerns about whether attending college is worth it for students. Families increasingly weigh tuition, financial aid, and borrowing against expected earnings after graduation, yet the relationships between these factors and long-term outcomes are complex and difficult to observe directly. This project uses the U.S. Department of Education’s College Scorecard dataset to investigate how institutional cost, student composition, and academic performance are associated with post-graduation earnings.

The analysis focuses on bachelor’s-degree-granting institutions and examines three main domains: cost of attendance (tuition and student debt), institutional characteristics (enrollment, sector, region, and locale), and student outcomes (retention, completion, and earnings). Two complementary modeling strategies are used. First, linear and penalized regression models estimate how these factors relate to median earnings ten years after enrollment. Second, logistic regression and random forest classifiers predict whether an institution falls above or below the sample median earnings level and identify which features are most important for classification. The goal is not to make causal claims, but to characterize patterns in the data and highlight which institutional features are most strongly associated with economic outcomes for graduates.
